caption:
Who carved Dighton Rock?

The rock is a 40-ton gray-brown sandstone boulder, about 5 feet high and 11 feet long, that sat in the bed of the Taunton River at Berkley, Massachusetts, with its inscribed face turned toward the water and covered at high tide.

In 1690 Cotton Mather wrote that the characters were "very deeply Engraved, no man alive knows How or When." Mather had never seen the rock. The first reliable description, by Greenwood in 1730, says the "indentures are not very considerable." Sewall in 1768 and Kendall in 1807 both said most of the lines were so effaced that reading them was "wholly subject to the fancy."

That did not stop the readings. Phoenicians, proposed by Ezra Stiles in 1783. Norse, proposed by Carl Christian Rafn in 1837 and rejected by archaeologists including T. D. Kendrick and Kenneth Feder. Portuguese, proposed by Edmund B. Delabarre in 1912, who read abbreviated Latin: "I, Miguel Cortereal, 1511. In this place, by the will of God, I became a chief of the Indians." Hunter (2017) debunked that origin myth. Chinese explorers, proposed by Gavin Menzies in 2002.

James Russell Lowell joked that candidates should write their letters in the Dighton script, "every fresh decipherer of which is enabled to educe a different meaning."

Still open: the carvings are of ancient and uncertain origin. American Indians are known to have inscribed petroglyphs in rocks, and a schematic face on Dighton Rock resembles one in Eastern Vermont. The boulder was lifted from the river in 1963 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971.

Images: Horatio B. King's 1853 daguerreotypes of Seth Eastman on the rock; Frank S. Davis's 1893 photograph; the 1830 survey drawing published 1844; an 1864 lithograph; and the museum today by Daderot.
